To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the proportion of C. burneti-seropositive primiparous dairy heifers in an endemic herd increased from 0% at the age of nine months to 100% after 100 DIM.
C. burneti seropositivity is not associated with post-partum diseases in heifers or primiparous dairy cattle.

the majority of primiparous cows were seronegativ and shed C. burnetti in milk or the genital tract, and that C. burnettii seroposivity and vaginal shedding had no impact but milk fat yield was decreased in puerperally vaginal shedders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the first report on C. burneti serology and shedding in primiparious cows in an endemic dairy herd and the impact on post-partum disease, fertility and milk yield.
the epidemiology of C. burnettii in a herd with high prevalence.
C. burneti serology and bacterial shedding in dairy heifers in an endemical infected herd.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the investigated herd is highly infected, that the heifers are not exposed to C. burnetti before the first parturition and that C. burnettii infection is not related to reproductive performance in this herd, but may be related to milk fat yield.

the presence of C. burneti in the genital tract and the serological response of primiparous cows are not a risk factor for reproductive performance, but may be associated with a reduced milk fat yield.
the impact of C. burneti on milk yield and reproduction is limited in primiparous cows.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
primiparous cows shed C. burneti during their first 150 DIM, which may be associated with a reduced milk fat yield.
the infection with C. burneti is not a risk factor for reproductive failure in dairy cows.

the presence of C. burneti DNA in vaginal secretions and the detection of specific antibodies in serum samples were common in heifers and cows of the studied herd and that the presence of specific C. burnetti antibodies in serum samples and the detection of C. urnetti DNA in milk samples were associated with a reduced milk fat yield.
The main takeaway from our work is that
C. burnetti shedding and seropositivity in heifers and first parity cows in a Q-fever-endemic dairy farm had no impact on reproductive parameters, but may have an influence on milk fat production.
C. burneti is a common infection in dairy herds, which is transmitted to calves during the first months of life, but is also transmitted from cows during parturition.
C. burnetti seroconversion and vaginal shedding are common in dairy heifers and primiparae in a herd with a high prevalence of C. burnettii.
